entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry IV of Castile (1425–1474), King of Castile and León from 1454 until his death, stands as a pivotal yet often maligned figure in the late medieval Iberian Peninsula. The last Castilian monarch of the Trastámara dynasty before the ascendance of the Catholic Monarchs, his reign was characterized by profound aristocratic instability, a weakening of royal authority, and a protracted succession crisis. His perceived inability to control the powerful Castilian nobility and the controversies surrounding his personal life and the legitimacy of his daughter, Joanna la Beltraneja, ultimately set the stage for the unification of Spain under Ferdinand and Isabella.

During his rule, Henry IV struggled to assert the crown's power against an increasingly assertive and factionalized aristocracy, led by figures like Juan Pacheco, Marqués de Villena. Efforts to reform the royal administration and finance were consistently undermined by noble leagues, culminating in the notorious "Farce of Ávila" in 1465, where an effigy of the king was ritually deposed by rebellious nobles who then proclaimed his half-brother, Alfonso, as the rightful monarch. This unprecedented challenge to royal legitimacy, fueled by allegations of Henry's impotence and Joanna's illegitimacy, plunged Castile into civil strife and demonstrated the extreme fragility of the monarchy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry IV's tumultuous reign, marked by profound aristocratic challenges and a succession crisis, directly led to the War of the Castilian Succession and ultimately paved the way for the dynastic union of Castile and Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs, forming the core of modern Spain.
